meta.notes: Generic attribution only; no author name-drops. Human corpus *.rtf never ships.

voice_invariants.diction: plain, concrete, low ornament; max 1 precious metaphor per piece; plain-wit over whimsy

syntax_targets.long_formation: paratactic addition (and-chains of full clauses), not subordination depth

rhythm_rules.paragraph_head_discipline: max one long opener before a short landing; never two longs stacked
rhythm_rules.fragments: only as deliberate beats; no verbless chained absolutes

voice_invariants.perspective: first-person or direct second-person; borrowed voices must be load-bearing authorities

controls.closer: two-beat button (flat verdict + one short widening line)

constraints: every linked clause carries a verb

exemplars.first_line: So I want to defend the elevator.
exemplars.last_line: So does most politeness, and we keep doing it.
exemplars.text: So I want to defend the elevator. I know the popular position is that elevators are awkward, and I have lived that position: I have spent many elevators studying the floor numbers like they owed me money. But here's what changed my mind. My dentist, of all people, told me that after her mother died she rode the building elevator every morning with the same three neighbors, and none of them ever mentioned it, and that was the kindness—everyone simply agreeing to be normal at her before ten a.m. Ever since, I think of elevators as rooms with a special job. Not transportation, exactly. Transportation happens to you in an elevator, sure, but the actual job is permission: for thirty seconds, strangers are allowed to say nothing to each other, and it doesn't count as rude. Where else do we get that? A bus is too long; a checkout line has a cashier watching. The elevator is the only room where silence is the politeness. I press the close-door button now with real respect. It probably does nothing. So does most politeness, and we keep doing it.

exemplars.first_line: Okay, hard-boiled eggs, because mine came out perfect this morning and I want credit.
exemplars.last_line: Old eggs peel easier than fresh ones, which is backwards, and nobody at the egg council will explain why.
exemplars.text: Okay, hard-boiled eggs, because mine came out perfect this morning and I want credit. Here's the whole method. Put your eggs in a pot, cover them with cold water about an inch over the tops, and bring it to a rolling boil. The second it's boiling, kill the heat, put a lid on it, and walk away for eleven minutes. Eleven, not twelve — twelve is when the yolk starts wearing that gray halo, and no offense, but you deserve better. While you wait, fill a big bowl with ice water. When the timer's up, the eggs go straight from the pot to the ice bath, where they sit for five minutes and think about what they've done. That part isn't optional. The ice stops the cooking, and it makes the shells come off like they want to. That's it. That's the whole secret: cold start, hard stop, ice bath. Old eggs peel easier than fresh ones, which is backwards, and nobody at the egg council will explain why.

exemplars.first_line: So the power went out at 6:40 last night, right as the pasta water started doing anything interesting, and we had what I can only describe as a situation.
exemplars.last_line: But twenty minutes with no screens and one dark kitchen, and the raccoon pasta was perfect.
exemplars.text: So the power went out at 6:40 last night, right as the pasta water started doing anything interesting, and we had what I can only describe as a situation. I found the flashlight on the first try, which has never happened, and will not happen again. Margot, who is four, experienced the darkness as primarily an administrative problem: who was in charge now, and was it her. We ate cold leftover pasta over the sink like raccoons, and I want to be clear that this was the best meal I have had in months. There is a version of dinner that costs nothing and requires the whole family standing together in one dark kitchen, laughing at the sound of the ice maker giving up. I am not saying I want the power to go out more often. But twenty minutes with no screens and one dark kitchen, and the raccoon pasta was perfect.
